headline: Two Massachusetts men avoid prison after Harvard Medical School explosion
dek: A federal judge sentenced Logan Patterson and Dominick Cardoza to probation and restitution for setting off a commercial firework inside a Harvard Medical School research building during Halloween weekend 2025.
body: Two Massachusetts men will not serve prison time for an explosion inside a Harvard Medical School building, but a federal judge has placed both on probation and ordered them to repay the medical school for the damage. Logan David Patterson, 19, of Plymouth, and Dominick Frank Cardoza, 21, of Bourne were sentenced Thursday in federal court in Boston, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Massachusetts. (https://www.justice.gov/usao-ma/pr/two-men-sentenced-causing-explosion-harvard-medical-school-campus)

U.S. District Judge Angel Kelley gave each defendant three years of probation and ordered the pair to pay $28,517 in restitution to Harvard Medical School. The sentence resolves a case that began after an early-morning blast on Nov. 1, 2025, at the Goldenson Building on the school’s Longwood Medical Area campus. The defendants had pleaded guilty in April to one count each of conspiring to damage a building by means of an explosive.

The government’s account, summarized in the sentencing announcement, places the men near the campus shortly after 2:20 a.m. Surveillance video showed two people in face coverings and dark clothing walking toward the medical school, then lighting what appeared to be Roman-candle fireworks. Prosecutors said the pair climbed into a construction area, used scaffolding to reach the roof and entered the building. At about 2:45 a.m., Harvard campus police received a fire-alarm alert tied to an explosion on the fourth floor.

The device was a large commercial firework placed inside a wooden locker in a fourth-floor research laboratory within Harvard Medical School’s Department of Neurobiology, federal prosecutors said. Video later showed the defendants on the fifth floor before they left through a first-floor emergency exit and ran in different directions. The U.S. Attorney’s Office said they discarded clothing associated with the incident and returned to the nearby Wentworth Institute of Technology, where they had been visiting for Halloween social activities. (https://www.justice.gov/usao-ma/pr/two-men-plead-guilty-causing-explosion-harvard-medical-school-campus)

No one was injured, but the blast triggered a major police response and public alarm around a Boston medical and academic campus. Boston.com reported that the men had been in the area for college Halloween events and that prosecutors argued the nighttime break-in, face coverings, property damage and flight warranted a period of home confinement. Judge Kelley declined that request, saying the felony convictions and other consequences were sufficient deterrence. (https://www.boston.com/news/crime/2026/10/02/mass-men-sentenced-harvard-explosion/)

The sentence also carries obligations beyond probation and restitution. Boston.com reported that each man was ordered to complete 300 hours of community service, and that the pair must write apology letters to Harvard. Patterson apologized in court, the outlet reported. The defendants had no prior criminal records, according to the report, but the felony convictions will continue to affect them after the case ends.

The case is significant locally because it turns a highly visible campus-security incident into a completed federal criminal proceeding without a prison term. The Goldenson Building houses a research laboratory, and the episode involved a construction area, a roof entry and an explosive device inside an occupied university complex, even though the building was empty when the firework was detonated. Those details explain why prosecutors sought additional restrictions despite the defendants’ guilty pleas and lack of prior record.

The defendants originally faced a statutory maximum of five years in prison, up to three years of supervised release and a fine of as much as $250,000, according to the April plea announcement. The confirmed next phase is therefore supervision, community service and restitution rather than incarceration. The federal sentencing release does not announce any further criminal hearing or a change to Harvard’s campus operations. (https://www.justice.gov/usao-ma/pr/two-men-plead-guilty-causing-explosion-harvard-medical-school-campus)
